title: Your First Vec
story: You're planning a party and need a guest list. At first you don't know how many people are coming — five? ten? fifty? A regular variable can only hold one name, but you need a list that grows as people RSVP. You need a Vec.
why: Vec is XIOM's growable array — the fundamental collection for storing ordered sequences of items that change size at runtime.
analogy: A Vec is like a grocery list on a whiteboard — you start with an empty board, write items one by one, and if you need more space, you just keep writing. The list grows to fit however many things you need to remember.
try_it: Create a Vec[Int] and push the numbers 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 into it. Print the length after each push to watch it grow. Then create a second Vec[Float64] with three decimal numbers and print its length. What happens if you try to push a string into a Vec[Int]?
tips: Always declare the type: `Vec[Int].new()` — the `[Int]` tells XIOM what kind of items the Vec holds
`.push()` adds to the END of the Vec — items stay in the order you added them
Use `.len()` not `.length` — XIOM uses `len` for all collection sizes
common_mistakes: Forgetting the type: `Vec.new()` won't compile — XIOM needs `Vec[Int].new()` or `Vec[Str].new()`
Using `=` instead of `.`: `colors = push("red")` is wrong — it's `colors.push("red")`
Trying to push a different type: once a Vec is `Vec[Int]`, every item must be an Int
